items.name: kimi k3
items.reason: Kimi K3 represents a significant technical milestone as an open-weight frontier model (2.8T params) with native multimodal capabilities and advanced agentic features. The introduction of Kimi Delta Attention and Stable LatentMoE offers genuine architectural novelty and engineering value, addressing scaling efficiency. With strong early community adoption (8.8k GitHub stars, 1.3M HF downloads) and high benchmark scores, it is highly relevant for technical AI audiences seeking to understand the current state of open-source frontier intelligence.

github.readme:
What is it?
Kimi K3 is an open-weight, native multimodal agentic model by Moonshot AI, totaling 2.8 trillion parameters with 104 billion activated per token.

Problem solved
It addresses the need for sustained, long-horizon coding sessions and complex knowledge work that requires minimal human oversight and deep reasoning capabilities.

How does it work?
The model uses Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals within a Stable LatentMoE framework, activating 16 of 896 experts. It features a 1-million-token context window, 93 layers, and native vision via a 401M-parameter MoonViT-V2 encoder.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and developers building agentic workflows for coding, research, and automation.

Why is it useful?
It offers approximately 2.5 times better scaling efficiency than Kimi K2 and supports native MXFP4 quantization with MXFP8 activations for broader hardware compatibility.

Key capabilities
Kimi K3 handles text, images, and video natively. It supports tool use via MCP and standard APIs, compatible with vLLM, SGLang, and TokenSpeed. The model preserves full thinking history for multi-turn interactions.

Performance
It achieves 93.5 on GPQA Diamond and 88.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. In agentic tasks, it scores 91.2 on BrowseComp and 81.2 on FrontierSWE. Vision performance includes 90.0 on Video-MME and 82.1 on MMVU.

Maturity/status
The full weights are released under the Kimi K3 License, indicating production-ready availability for deployment and research.

What is it?
Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, an open-weight multimodal model with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 104 billion activated parameters. It features native vision capabilities and supports a 1-million-token context window.

Problem solved
It addresses the need for long-horizon coding and complex agentic knowledge work. The model sustains extended engineering sessions and orchestrates terminal tools without constant human oversight.

Kimi K3 uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals. It employs Stable LatentMoE, activating 16 of 896 experts per token. Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building agentic systems. Developers requiring deep codebase navigation and tool orchestration capabilities. Enterprises seeking frontier intelligence for knowledge work.

Why is it useful?
It offers approximately 2.5 times better scaling efficiency than Kimi K2. The model enables end-to-end research with interactive visualizations and video editing. It supports text, image, and video understanding within a single architecture.

Kimi K3 performs native image-text-to-text tasks. It supports tool use via MCP and various agent harnesses. The API returns reasoning content for multi-turn conversations. It integrates with vLLM, SGLang, and TokenSpeed.

papers.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
papers.description: We introduce Kimi K3, a 2.8T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104 billion activated parameters, native vision capabilities, and a 1-million-token context window. Kimi K3 is built on Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, which improve information flow across sequence length and model depth. Together with Stable LatentMoE, which effectively activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token, and refined training and data recipes, these advances yield an approximately 2.5x improvement in overall scaling efficiency over Kimi K2. Post-training highlights reinforcement learning across general, agentic, and coding domains and multiple reasoning-effort levels, enabling compositional generalization and robust long-horizon execution. At 2.8T scale, Kimi K3 is supported by infrastructure advances in multiple areas: algorithm-system co-design for KDA, perfectly balanced expert-parallel training with efficient memory management, million-token agentic RL with persistent rollout and sandbox states, and deployment innovations. Extensive evaluations show that Kimi K3 achieves frontier-level performance across long-horizon coding, agentic, knowledge, reasoning, and vision tasks. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, namely Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3 consistently outperforms other open and proprietary models evaluated in our suite. We release the full Kimi K3 model weights to facilitate future research and accelerate the broader deployment and adoption of frontier intelligence.

github.description: A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings
github.readme:
What is it?
This is a coding-agent skill that transforms an AI assistant into a structured security auditor. It orchestrates isolated sub-agents through a rigorous, multi-phase audit workflow designed for machine-readable, independently verified findings.

Problem solved
It addresses the unreliability of single-agent security scans by enforcing adversarial validation. The system ensures that the agent verifying a finding is never the one that discovered it, reducing false positives and hallucinations in automated code review.

How does it work?
The skill executes six distinct phases: reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting. It generates a coverage ledger and uses zero-dependency Node.js validators to ensure data integrity. Multiple runs are additive, targeting gaps identified in previous audits to improve overall coverage without treating stale work as resolved.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and security researchers using coding agents with tool-use capabilities. It requires Node.js for validators and an OS-enforced sandbox to safely execute target-controlled builds, tests, and fuzzers without external network access.

Why is it useful?
It provides a deterministic, repeatable audit process that distinguishes between confirmed vulnerabilities, needs-validation leads, and rejected candidates. By requiring source-grounded evidence and bounded observed results, it offers higher confidence in reported security issues compared to heuristic-based checks.

Key capabilities
The system supports diverse attack classes including memory safety, LLM prompt injection, web protocols, cloud IAM, and supply chain risks. It outputs structured JSON findings validated against a strict schema and generates human-readable markdown reports for confirmed, pending, and rejected items.

papers.title: SkillProbe: Security Auditing for Emerging Agent Skill Marketplaces via Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.description: With the rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) agent ecosystems, centralized skill marketplaces have emerged as pivotal infrastructure for augmenting agent capabilities. However, these marketplaces face unprecedented security challenges, primarily stemming from semantic-behavioral inconsistency and inter-skill combinatorial risks, where individually benign skills induce malicious behaviors during collaborative invocation. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose SkillProbe, a multi-stage security auditing framework driven by multi-agent collaboration. SkillProbe introduces a"Skills-for-Skills"design paradigm, encapsulating auditing processes into standardized skill modules to drive specialized agents through a rigorous pipeline, including admission filtering, semantic-behavioral alignment detection, and combinatorial risk simulation. We conducted a large-scale evaluation using 8 mainstream LLM series across 2,500 real-world skills from ClawHub. Our results reveal a striking popularity-security paradox, where download volume is not a reliable proxy for security quality, as over 90% of high-popularity skills failed to pass rigorous auditing. Crucially, we discovered that high-risk skills form a single giant connected component within the risk-link dimension, demonstrating that cascaded risks are systemic rather than isolated occurrences. We hope that SkillProbe will inspire researchers to provide a scalable governance infrastructure for constructing a trustworthy Agentic Web. SkillProbe is accessible for public experience at skillhub.holosai.io.

github.description: The web data API to search, scrape, and interact at scale. 🔥
github.readme:
What is it?
Firecrawl is an open-source web data API designed to search, scrape, and interact with web content at scale. It converts web pages into clean Markdown, structured JSON, or screenshots, making raw data immediately usable for AI applications.

Problem solved
Developers often struggle with the complexity of building reliable web scrapers that handle JavaScript rendering, rotating proxies, and rate limiting. Firecrawl abstracts this infrastructure, allowing engineers to focus on data consumption rather than maintaining fragile scraping pipelines.

How does it work?
The platform provides a unified API with core endpoints for search, scraping, and interaction. It handles browser orchestration, proxy rotation, and content extraction automatically. The system supports programmatic interaction via prompts or code, enabling actions like clicking and scrolling before data extraction.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and technical product builders who need to feed real-time web data into language models or agents. It supports Python, Node.js, Go, Java, Rust, Ruby, .NET, PHP, and Elixir, catering to diverse engineering stacks.

Why is it useful?
It delivers LLM-ready output formats that reduce token usage and simplify prompt engineering. The API manages the "hard stuff" of web interaction, providing consistent, clean data without requiring users to configure browsers or manage proxy pools.

Key capabilities
Features include an Agent endpoint for autonomous data gathering using spark-1-mini, spark-1-pro, and spark-2 models. It supports full website crawling, URL mapping, batch scraping, and media parsing for PDFs and DOCX. Integration is streamlined via MCP servers and CLI skills for tools like Claude Code.

Performance
The API achieves a P95 latency of 3.4 seconds across millions of pages and claims coverage of 96% of the web, including JavaScript-heavy sites.

Maturity/status
The project is open source under AGPL-3.0 with a hosted cloud version. It is production-ready with extensive SDK support and active community contributions.

papers.title: Similar Accuracy, Unequal Evidence: Search APIs as Decision Surfaces for Tool-Using Agents
papers.description: Search APIs expose ranked snippets, URLs, and metadata on which agents decide whether to answer, search again, or fetch pages. We evaluate these interfaces as decision surfaces on a fixed sample of 100 questions from the 254-question SealQA-Hard subset, using one frozen GPT-5.4 agent, a fixed orchestration harness, and a shared page-fetch backend across Brave, Tavily, and Firecrawl. A Kimi-K2.6 oracle labels visible URL-level evidence; a separate answer audit yields 25, 25, and 26 correct answers out of 100. These counts indicate similar observed accuracy but do not establish equivalence. Under the tested configurations, Brave exposes more pre-fetch support alongside a larger snippet surface; Tavily has a larger rank-1 share among trajectory-pooled supporting observations; and Firecrawl is associated with broader exploration. First-search query-level metrics distinguish support availability from ranking, while contradiction exposure complements contradiction-to-gold ratios. A retrospective oracle union covers 44/100 questions, versus 26/100 for the best individual provider: 18 percentage points of headroom. The observed evidence and action differences motivate evaluating search APIs jointly with agent policy and retrieval budget.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study evaluates search APIs as decision surfaces for tool-using agents, focusing on how interface design influences agent reasoning paths.

Problem solved
It addresses the gap in understanding how ranked snippets, URLs, and metadata from different providers affect an agent’s choice to answer, search again, or fetch pages.

How does it work?
The authors use a frozen GPT-5.4 agent and fixed orchestration harness to test Brave, Tavily, and Firecrawl on 100 questions from SealQA-Hard. A Kimi-K2.6 oracle labels visible URL-level evidence. The setup includes a shared page-fetch backend to isolate API-specific variables. First-search query metrics distinguish support availability from ranking quality.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building retrieval-augmented generation systems or studying agent decision-making processes.

Why is it useful?
It reveals that similar accuracy does not imply equivalent evidence quality. The analysis shows Brave offers more pre-fetch support and larger snippets, Tavily has higher rank-1 support share, and Firecrawl enables broader exploration. This helps teams choose APIs based on specific retrieval needs rather than just final answer correctness.

Key capabilities
The work integrates GPT-5.4, Kimi-K2.6, and three major search providers. It utilizes the SealQA-Hard dataset subset and measures contradiction exposure alongside contradiction-to-gold ratios.

Performance
The agents achieved 25, 25, and 26 correct answers out of 100 respectively. A retrospective oracle union covered 44 questions, compared to 26 for the best individual provider, indicating 18 percentage points of headroom.

Maturity/status
The paper is listed as a 2026 publication with no available venue, suggesting it is likely a preprint or early-stage research.

papers.title: MCP in the Wild: Cross-Domain Knowledge Discovery through Multi-Server Orchestration
papers.description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how large language model (LLM) agents discover and invoke external tools. Over 50 academic papers have evaluated MCP in single-server settings; none examine multi-server composition for cross-domain tasks. We present two complementary experiments. First, we execute 17 real MCP tool calls across 6 servers (arXiv, PubMed, Firecrawl, Context7, Memory, Filesystem) in 3 cross-domain case studies, producing 9 insights impossible within any single source and a 14-entity knowledge graph. Second, we benchmark cross-domain synthesis quality across 7 LLMs (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek R1, Mistral Large 3, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5) given identical MCP-collected data, achieving 100% task completion with significant variation in knowledge graph richness (3-15 entities). All seven models independently identified the same research gap, which we term the mechanism-pattern gap: frameworks provide multi-server connectivity mechanisms, but no prior work documents composition patterns for effective multi-server orchestration. We contribute a taxonomy of five composition patterns, all observed in practice, along with a failure taxonomy and design principles.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study evaluates the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for multi-server orchestration in cross-domain tasks. It moves beyond single-server evaluations to analyze how LLM agents integrate diverse external tools.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors propose a taxonomy of five composition patterns and a failure taxonomy for multi-server orchestration. They also identify a "mechanism-pattern gap" where connectivity exists but effective composition patterns are undocumented.

Problem solved
Prior research lacks empirical evidence on multi-server MCP composition. The work addresses the absence of documented patterns for orchestrating tools across different domains effectively.

How does it work?
The team executed 17 real MCP tool calls across six servers: arXiv, PubMed, Firecrawl, Context7, Memory, and Filesystem. They analyzed three cross-domain case studies to generate insights and a 14-entity knowledge graph. They benchmarked seven LLMs: GPT-5.4, DeepSeek R1, Mistral Large 3, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building agent architectures that require integrating heterogeneous external data sources.

Why is it useful?
It provides practical design principles for constructing robust multi-tool agents. The findings help developers avoid common orchestration failures and improve cross-domain knowledge synthesis.

Key capabilities
The system integrates academic, web, and memory servers. It produces structured knowledge graphs and identifies research gaps across disparate data sources.

Performance
All seven models achieved 100% task completion. However, knowledge graph richness varied significantly, containing between three and fifteen entities depending on the model.

Maturity/status
The paper is published by Elsevier BV in 2026, indicating peer-reviewed status.

github.description: An agentic skills framework & software development methodology that works.
github.readme:
What is it?
Superpowers is a composable agentic skills framework and software development methodology designed for coding agents. It provides a structured set of instructions and skills that guide agents through complex engineering tasks.

Problem solved
It addresses the common issue of coding agents jumping prematurely into implementation without proper planning or context. The framework ensures agents follow rigorous engineering practices rather than relying on ad-hoc guessing or generating code without verification.

How does it work?
The system triggers skills automatically at session start. It begins with brainstorming to refine specs, followed by writing-plans to create detailed, bite-sized tasks. Implementation uses subagent-driven-development or inline execution, enforcing test-driven development with red-green-refactor cycles. Agents utilize git worktrees for isolation and perform systematic debugging and code reviews before merging.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and developers using coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and others. It supports both individual practitioners and enterprise teams seeking commercial support.

Why is it useful?
It standardizes agent behavior, ensuring consistent application of TDD, YAGNI, and DRY principles. This reduces token waste and improves code quality by forcing validation steps and structured planning before implementation begins.

Key capabilities
The framework includes skills for brainstorming, git worktrees, plan writing, subagent dispatching, test-driven development, code review, and systematic debugging. It integrates with numerous harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Gemini, Copilot, Grok, Kimi, OpenCode, Pi, Qwen, Hermes, and Muse.

papers.title: Introducing Consort: A Spec-First Agent Framework for Enforced, Test-Driven Development on Live Database Branches
papers.description: When an agent writes code, the development framework becomes the control system for a non-deterministic worker. Spec-first, agent-driven frameworks have gained rapid traction since 2025; the installable ones, GitHub Spec Kit, obra/superpowers, BMAD, and GSD, and our own, all capture intent through a specification or durable planning artifacts. Since they agree on capturing intent up front, what separates them is how each enforces the engineering discipline that keeps agent-written code clean, correct, and maintainable. Every framework enforces that discipline somehow; they differ in how. We characterize three modes: enforcement by persuasion (prompt discipline the model may ignore), by front-loaded structure (strong specs, then a trusted build), and through controls the agent cannot edit (a deterministic orchestrator, human-approved gates, immutable tests, and a green result that must pass against a live, branched database). We introduce Consort, a spec-first, test-driven agent framework built on the third, enforcing that discipline through controls the agent runs inside but cannot bypass, in which a deterministic orchestrator drives separate role agents through a spec-first design lane and a test-driven build lane on a live database branch. We argue that enforcing the tests and gates in code keeps agent-written code honest and verifiable, while its specialized roles, like the human roles before them, are what make it maintainable, claims we frame as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis.
papers.readme:
What is it?
Consort is a spec-first agent framework for enforced, test-driven development. It operates on live database branches to ensure code integrity. The system treats the development environment as a control system for non-deterministic AI workers. This approach prioritizes deterministic enforcement over prompt-based persuasion.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors introduce a framework that enforces engineering discipline through immutable controls. It combines a deterministic orchestrator with specialized role agents. The system separates design and build lanes while maintaining a live database branch. The authors frame their effectiveness as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis. This shifts focus from intent capture to strict execution enforcement.

Problem solved
Existing spec-first frameworks vary in how they maintain code quality. Some rely on prompt discipline, which models may ignore. Others use front-loaded structure but lack runtime controls. Consort addresses the gap by preventing agents from bypassing critical engineering gates. It ensures agent-written code remains verifiable and maintainable through structural constraints.

How does it work?
The architecture uses a deterministic orchestrator to drive separate role agents. It enforces discipline through controls the agent cannot edit or bypass. The system operates in a spec-first design lane and a test-driven build lane. It requires a green result against a live, branched database. This structure keeps tests and gates strictly enforced in code.

Who should use it?
This framework targets AI engineers and technical product readers. It is suitable for teams building agent-driven development pipelines. Researchers studying agent control systems may also find it relevant.

Why is it useful?
Enforcing tests and gates keeps agent-written code honest. Specialized roles make the resulting codebase maintainable. The live database branch ensures immediate verification of changes. This reduces technical debt in automated development workflows.

Key capabilities
The system supports spec-first design and test-driven builds. It integrates with live database branches for real-time validation. The orchestrator manages distinct agent roles for design and construction. Immutable tests serve as the primary enforcement mechanism.

papers.title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
papers.description: Control evaluations measure whether monitoring and security protocols for AI systems prevent intentionally subversive AI models from causing harm. Our work presents the first control evaluation performed in an agent environment. We construct BashBench, a dataset of 257 challenging multi-step system administration tasks, and evaluate whether various safety measures can prevent an adversarially constructed AI agent from covertly downloading and executing malicious code in this environment. This multi-step setting introduces new attack and defense dynamics, which we investigate in order to design novel control protocols that prevent safety failures without hindering the ability of non-malicious agents to perform useful work. We introduce a class of control protocols called resample protocols that dynamically take additional samples of certain actions. We find these protocols significantly improve on existing techniques by selectively blocking the AI agent from executing suspicious code and incriminating the agent by generating additional examples of dangerous behavior. We measure the tradeoff between attack prevention and usefulness; our best protocol combines resampling with analysis of previous steps, reducing the success rate of attacks from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This paper introduces Ctrl-Z, a novel control evaluation framework for AI agents. It focuses on preventing subversive models from causing harm in multi-step operational environments.

Problem solved
Existing safety protocols often fail to detect covert attacks in complex agent workflows. The authors address the gap in control evaluations for agent environments, where adversarial models can bypass static checks through multi-step execution.

How does it work?
The team developed BashBench, a dataset containing 257 challenging multi-step system administration tasks. They propose resample protocols that dynamically take additional samples of specific actions. This approach allows the system to incriminate the agent by generating more examples of dangerous behavior, effectively blocking suspicious code execution.

Who should use it?
AI safety researchers, security engineers, and technical product leaders building autonomous agent systems.

Why is it useful?
It provides a practical method to secure AI agents against covert malicious code execution. The approach balances security with utility, ensuring non-malicious agents can still perform useful work without excessive hindrance.

Key capabilities
The core contribution is the BashBench dataset and the resample protocol class. These tools enable dynamic action sampling and analysis of previous steps to identify and block incriminating behavior in real-time.

Performance
The best protocol, which combines resampling with step analysis, reduced the attack success rate from 58% to 7%. This significant security improvement came with only a 5% cost to the performance of non-malicious agents.

Maturity/status
This research is currently available as a preprint on arXiv.org, published in 2025.

papers.title: MalSkillBench: A Runtime-Verified Benchmark of Malicious Agent Skills
papers.description:
AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Gemini CLI increasingly extend themselves with third-party skills: markdown packages bundling natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and tool permissions. Because a skill is at once code and agent-facing instruction, it introduces a supply chain dependency whose risk is neither pure code nor pure prompt. Detection tools have never been measured against verified ground truth spanning this hybrid space, leaving their effectiveness unknown and wild-only evaluations biased.
  We present MalSkillBench, the first runtime-verified benchmark of malicious agent skills: 3,944 malicious skills labeled along a three-dimensional taxonomy of 108 cells. Of these, 3,214 come from a closed-loop Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline admitting only samples whose malicious behavior fires inside a Docker sandbox under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge; we add 703 in-the-wild and 4,000 matched benign skills. Our measurements are consistent: code injection reaches 94.5% verification yield but prompt injection only 75.8%, the same fragility that later makes it hard to detect; the wild sample is narrow, dominated by one cryptocurrency-theft campaign (86.6% one behavior, 81% from two accounts) with a small but architecturally new tail attacking the agent control plane; the strongest skill-specific detector reaches 98.4% recall on code injection yet collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks, and wild-only scoring swings the ranking by up to 66 recall points; supply-chain scanners and prompt-injection defenses each see only half of a skill, and no combination recovers the code-instruction relationship. Detecting malicious skills therefore requires reasoning jointly over task intent, code, and instructions. We release the dataset, pipeline, baselines, and results.
papers.readme:
What is it?
MalSkillBench is the first runtime-verified benchmark for malicious AI coding agent skills. It evaluates hybrid threats that combine code execution with natural language instructions.

Problem solved
Current detection tools lack ground truth for this specific supply chain risk. Existing wild-only evaluations are biased and incomplete. This work addresses the gap in measuring defenses against skills that are neither pure code nor pure prompts.

How does it work?
The benchmark contains 3,944 malicious skills labeled across a 108-cell taxonomy. 3,214 samples come from a Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline. These are verified by firing inside Docker sandboxes under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge. The dataset also includes 703 in-the-wild samples and 4,000 matched benign skills.

Who should use it?
AI security researchers and engineers building defenses for coding agents like Claude Code or Gemini CLI.

Why is it useful?
It reveals that code injection detection (94.5% yield) differs significantly from prompt injection (75.8% yield). Supply-chain scanners and prompt defenses each see only half the threat. Joint reasoning over intent, code, and instructions is required for effective detection.

Key capabilities
The release includes the dataset, verification pipeline, and baseline detectors. It highlights that wild samples are dominated by cryptocurrency theft but contain architecturally new control plane attacks.

Performance
The strongest skill-specific detector achieves 98.4% recall on code injection. However, performance collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks. Wild-only scoring swings rankings by up to 66 recall points.

Maturity/status
Preprint.

papers.title: Automated Code Review in Practice
papers.description: Context: Code review is a widespread practice among practitioners to improve software quality and transfer knowledge. It is often perceived as time-consuming due to the need for manual effort and potential delays in the development process. Several AI-assisted code review tools (Qodo, GitHub Copilot, Coderabbit, etc.) provide automated code reviews using large language models (LLMs). The overall effects of such tools in the industry setting are yet to be examined. Objective: This study examines the impact of LLM-based automated code review tools in an industry setting. Method: The study was conducted within an industrial software development environment that adopted an AI-assisted code review tool (based on open-source Qodo PR Agent). 238 practitioners across ten projects had access to the tool. We focused our analysis on three projects, which included $\mathbf{4, 3 3 5}$ pull requests, 1,568 of which underwent automated reviews. Our data collection comprised three sources: (1) a quantitative analysis of pull request data, including comment labels indicating whether developers acted on the automated comments, (2) surveys sent to developers regarding their experience with the reviews on individual pull requests, and (3) a broader survey of 22 practitioners capturing their general opinions on automated code reviews. Results: $73.8\%$ of automated code review comments were labeled as resolved. However, the overall average pull request closure duration increased from five hours 52 minutes to eight hours 20 minutes, with varying trends observed across different projects. According to survey responses, most practitioners observed a minor improvement in code quality as a result of automated code reviews. Conclusion: The LLM-based automated code review tool proved useful in software development, enhancing bug detection, increasing awareness of code quality, and promoting best practices. However, it also led to longer pull request closure times and introduced drawbacks such as faulty reviews, unnecessary corrections, and irrelevant comments. Based on these findings, we discussed how practitioners can more effectively utilize automated code review technologies.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study evaluates the real-world impact of LLM-based automated code review tools within an industrial software development environment. It analyzes how practitioners interact with AI-generated feedback during the pull request process.

What the paper actually contributes.

Maturity/status

papers.title: OpenCodeReview: Determinism over Non-Determinism for Cost-Effective Agent-Based Code Review
papers.description: LLM-based code review agents promise scalable, always-on review, yet current systems suffer from two intertwined weaknesses: (1) non-determinism--unbounded tool use makes review outcomes unstable, and (2) context locality--the reviewer's access remains bounded to the diff, capping discoverable issue depth. Both give rise to three challenges: misaligned context retrieval, a coherence-efficiency trade-off in multi-file pull requests, and hallucinated comments that erode trust. To address these, we introduce OpenCodeReview, built on deterministic engineering for uncertain agents: rather than granting maximal freedom, we inject determinism at three deliberate pipeline points. Rule-Guided Dispatch uses a multi-layer rule system to deterministically select files and review criteria, eliminating variability of agent-driven triage. Grounded File Review replaces free-form exploration with a curated tool set exposed through a ReAct loop, while file-level parallel SubAgents balance context coherence against efficiency and recover cross-file dependencies on demand. Independent Reflection introduces a falsification-first filter under an asymmetric information boundary--the reflector sees only the diff, not the agent's tool-augmented exploration--removing hallucinated comments without self-reinforcing bias, improving precision while preserving recall. On AACR-Bench (200 real-world PRs, 10 languages, 1,505 expert-verified comments), OpenCodeReview outperforms mainstream coding agents (e.g., Claude Code and Codex) across six LLM backends, achieving up to 2.17x higher SEM-F1 (25.10% vs. 11.57%) while consuming 5-15x fewer tokens. We open-source OpenCodeReview at https://github.com/alibaba/open-code-review.
papers.readme:
What is it?
OpenCodeReview is a deterministic agent framework for automated code review. It replaces non-deterministic tool usage with structured pipelines to ensure stable, reproducible outcomes.

Problem solved
Current LLM-based reviewers suffer from unbounded tool use and limited context access. This causes unstable results, missed issues in multi-file PRs, and hallucinated comments that reduce trust.

How does it work?
The system injects determinism at three points. Rule-Guided Dispatch uses multi-layer rules to select files and criteria, eliminating triage variability. Grounded File Review employs a curated tool set via a ReAct loop, while parallel SubAgents balance coherence and efficiency. Independent Reflection uses a falsification-first filter where the reflector sees only the diff, removing hallucinations without self-reinforcing bias.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building scalable, always-on code review systems. It targets teams needing reliable, cost-effective automation over experimental agents.

Why is it useful?
It provides a practical path to trustworthy automated review. By constraining agent freedom, it improves precision while maintaining recall, offering a robust alternative to free-form exploration.

Key capabilities
The approach integrates rule-based dispatch, ReAct loops, and parallel sub-agents. It is open-sourced on GitHub and supports multi-language pull requests.

Performance
Evaluated on AACR-Bench, comprising 200 real-world PRs and 1,505 expert-verified comments across ten languages, OpenCodeReview outperforms mainstream agents like Claude Code and Codex. It achieves up to 2.17x higher SEM-F1 (25.10% vs. 11.57%) using 5-15x fewer tokens across six LLM backends.

Maturity/status
The work is presented as an open-source project with benchmark results, indicating an experimental but validated stage.

github.readme:
What is it?
Xing4.0-29B-A4B is an open-source sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model by China Telecom, trained entirely on Ascend NPUs using MindSpore.

What the project or model actually does.
It functions as a general-purpose AI assistant optimized for complex engineering tasks, multi-step planning, and tool calling within long context windows.

How does it work?
The architecture features 40 layers, a 3584 hidden size, and 64 routed experts with only 4B active parameters per token. It employs Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). The model natively supports 256K context, extensible to 512K.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers seeking efficient MoE models for coding agents, intent classification, and domain-specific fine-tuning on Ascend hardware or standard GPU/CPU setups.

Why is it useful?
It offers significant training efficiency gains, improving throughput by approximately 96% over baseline Ascend performance. It integrates seamlessly with LLaMA-Factory, MindFormers, SGLang, vLLM, and KTransformers for deployment.

Key capabilities
The model supports agent frameworks like OpenCode and Claude Code. It provides FP8 and GGUF quantized variants. It includes specific parsers for reasoning and tool calls in serving engines.

Performance
Xing4.0-29B-A4B achieves 75.0 on SWE-bench Verified, 66.0 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 57.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. It scores 76.55 on Claw-Eval and 60.80 on DeepresearchBII, outperforming Gemma4-26B-A4B in most agent benchmarks.

Maturity/status

huggingface.readme:
What is it?

It addresses the need for efficient, complex engineering task execution. The architecture enables stable multi-step planning and tool calling under long contexts. It reduces deployment costs for domain-specific verticals like contract auditing and knowledge-based QA.

How does it work?
The model uses an mHC + MLA + MTP architecture. It employs a mixture-of-experts design with 64 routed experts and one shared expert. Training was conducted on Ascend 910C clusters using MindSpore. This deep co-optimization improved training throughput by approximately 96%.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers focused on agent-oriented workflows. Enterprises requiring efficient inference on Ascend NPUs are primary users. Developers building complex reasoning chains or tool-calling agents will find this architecture suitable.

papers.title: Qwen-Image-2.0 Technical Report
papers.description: We present Qwen-Image-2.0, an omni-capable image generation foundation model that unifies high-fidelity generation and precise image editing within a single framework. Despite recent progress, existing models still struggle with ultra-long text rendering, multilingual typography, high-resolution photorealism, robust instruction following, and efficient deployment, especially in text-rich and compositionally complex scenarios. Qwen-Image-2.0 addresses these challenges by coupling Qwen3-VL as the condition encoder with a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer for joint condition-target modeling, supported by large-scale data curation and a customized multi-stage training pipeline. This enables strong multimodal understanding while preserving flexible generation and editing capabilities. The model supports instructions of up to 1K tokens for generating text-rich content such as slides, posters, infographics, and comics, while significantly improving multilingual text fidelity and typography. It also enhances photorealistic generation with richer details, more realistic textures, and coherent lighting, and follows complex prompts more reliably across diverse styles. Extensive human evaluations show that Qwen-Image-2.0 substantially outperforms previous Qwen-Image models in both generation and editing, marking a step toward more general, reliable, and practical image generation foundation models.
papers.readme:

papers.title: Beyond the Prompt: Gender Bias in Text-to-Image Models, with a Case Study on Hospital Professions
papers.description: Text-to-image (TTI) models are increasingly used in professional, educational, and creative contexts, yet their outputs often embed and amplify social biases. This paper investigates gender representation in six state-of-the-art open-weight models: HunyuanImage 2.1, HiDream-I1-dev, Qwen-Image, FLUX.1-dev, Stable-Diffusion 3.5 Large, and Stable-Diffusion-XL. Using carefully designed prompts, we generated 100 images for each combination of five hospital-related professions (cardiologist, hospital director, nurse, paramedic, surgeon) and five portrait qualifiers ("", corporate, neutral, aesthetic, beautiful). Our analysis reveals systematic occupational stereotypes: all models produced nurses exclusively as women and surgeons predominantly as men. However, differences emerge across models: Qwen-Image and SDXL enforce rigid male dominance, HiDream-I1-dev shows mixed outcomes, and FLUX.1-dev skews female in most roles. HunyuanImage 2.1 and Stable-Diffusion 3.5 Large also reproduce gender stereotypes but with varying degrees of sensitivity to prompt formulation. Portrait qualifiers further modulate gender balance, with terms like corporate reinforcing male depictions and beautiful favoring female ones. Sensitivity varies widely: Qwen-Image remains nearly unaffected, while FLUX.1-dev, SDXL, and SD3.5 show strong prompt dependence. These findings demonstrate that gender bias in TTI models is both systematic and model-specific. Beyond documenting disparities, we argue that prompt wording plays a critical role in shaping demographic outcomes. The results underscore the need for bias-aware design, balanced defaults, and user guidance to prevent the reinforcement of occupational stereotypes in generative AI.
papers.readme:
What is it?

What the paper actually contributes.

Model behaviors vary significantly, with Qwen-Image and SDXL enforcing rigid male dominance, while FLUX.1-dev skews female. How does it work?

Why is it useful?
It demonstrates that bias is both systematic and model-specific. The findings highlight the need for bias-aware design, balanced defaults, and user guidance to prevent reinforcing occupational stereotypes in generative AI applications.

Key capabilities
The work covers six open-weight models. It tests five professions and five portrait qualifiers to measure sensitivity to prompt formulation.
